analysis.one_liner: Requires public companies to get shareholder approval before spending company money on politics, and to disclose it.
analysis.headline: The Shareholder Protection Act never got a vote: 16 Democratic senators sponsored it, it was referred to the Banking Committee, and no action followed before Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required publicly traded companies to let their shareholders vote on whether the company can spend money on politics — independent campaign ads, electioneering communications, and dues to trade groups that often fund political activity anonymously. Companies would have to report every political expenditure quarterly and post each board member's vote on spending over $50,000 within 48 hours. Officers who spent shareholder money without approval would face personal liability for triple the amount. The bill died in the Senate Banking Committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Shareholders who own public companies — who currently have no way to know or control how corporate managers spend company money on elections and political causes — and voters, who would gain a public record of which corporations funded which candidates through which channels, including trade associations.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Shareholders and voters who track corporate money

how_it_helps.text: Requires a majority vote of shareholders before a company spends money on independent expenditures, electioneering communications, or payments to trade associations that could be used for politics [S3].
Treats unauthorized political spending as a breach of fiduciary duty, with officers and directors personally liable for three times the amount spent [S3].

Requires public companies to file quarterly reports naming each political expenditure, its date and amount, the candidate supported or opposed, and the trade associations receiving dues that could fund political activity [S3].
Requires board votes and 48-hour public disclosure of each director's vote on political spending above $50,000, and lets the SEC bar stock listing for non-compliant companies [S3].
Requires institutional investment managers to disclose annually how they voted on shareholder authorization of political spending, published through the SEC's EDGAR system [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Corporate boards and executives, who lose unilateral control over spending company money on elections; trade associations and 501(c) groups, whose political funding from corporate dues would no longer stay hidden; and public companies generally, which bear the cost of new compliance, voting, and reporting systems.

drawbacks.text: The bill excludes direct lobbying by registered lobbyists from the spending that requires shareholder approval, leaving a major and influential channel of corporate political money untouched [S3].
Public companies would face real compliance costs: annual shareholder votes, board voting procedures, quarterly and annual political-spending reports, and 48-hour disclosure duties [S3].
The rules apply only to publicly traded companies, so political money could shift to private firms and other vehicles outside the bill's reach [S3].

Critics of shareholder-approval schemes generally argue they add friction to company governance and can be dominated by a few large institutional managers; the bill tries to counter this by requiring those managers to disclose their votes publicly [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is simple: shareholders and voters gain control and visibility over corporate political money, while corporate managers and trade associations lose discretion and anonymity. The main honest objections are that direct lobbying stays untouched, that rules limited to public companies can push money into unregulated channels, and that compliance is a real cost. As a transparency measure it addresses one of the largest and least visible streams of money in federal elections.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in August 2017 and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never took it up; no hearing, no vote, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Senator Menendez introduced the bill on August 2, 2017 with 15 Democratic cosponsors [S1].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs on August 2, 2017 [S5].
No further action was recorded — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporate boards and executives keep unilateral control over spending shareholder money on politics, and trade associations keep receiving corporate dues that can fund political activity without shareholder consent or disclosure. Voters and shareholders get none of the visibility the bill promised.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 senators who signed on were Democrats; no Republican cosponsor joined, and the Republican-majority Banking Committee never acted on it [S4][S5].

industries.note: Executives and directors would lose unilateral power to spend company money on elections and would face triple-damages personal liability for unauthorized spending. Their control over other people's money is the main thing standing between voters and visibility into this spending stream.

Corporate dues to these groups are a major channel for political spending that shareholders and voters cannot trace; the bill would force identification of any association receiving dues that could fund political activity. Keeping that channel anonymous is why it exists.

Managers subject to SEC 13(f) reporting would have to disclose annually how they voted on shareholder authorization of political spending, published on EDGAR. The bill also gives them a legal safe harbor protecting divestment decisions made in response to a company's political spending.

Companies would bear compliance costs for shareholder votes, board procedures, and quarterly reporting, but shareholders — the companies' owners — would gain control over how their money is used politically.
